data.topic: The full story behind a prospector's horrifying 1874 ordeal in Colorado's San Juan Mountains — what really happened, beyond what this video tells

skim_summary: Alfred Packer entered the Colorado mountains with five men in winter 1874 and emerged alone two months later looking well-nourished.
Packer offered contradictory accounts regarding how his companions died and how he acquired their personal possessions and money.
Physical evidence from the crime scene and coroner findings contradicted Packer's claims of self-defense and gradual starvation.
Packer avoided original murder charges due to a legal technicality regarding Colorado's territorial laws, ultimately receiving a manslaughter conviction.
Public perception and legal outcomes shifted over time, influenced by media campaigns and mixed modern forensic findings.
sources.full_text:
In 1874, six men set off into Colorado's
San Juan Mountains in the middle of winter with the hopes of reaching some newly discovered
goldfields on the other side. Two months later, only a single man
emerged from the mountains, but instead of being emaciated as early
explorers were often later found, the man looked to be weirdly fed. This is the story of Alfred Packer, also known
as the Colorado Cannibal. As a quick note, although the descriptions
of the events in this video are fleeting and non-descriptive, they are still disturbing,
so viewer discretion is strongly advised. [intro music] On the morning of April 16th, 1874, the men who worked at Los Piños Indian Agency
near Saguache, Colorado were sitting and eating breakfast
when the mess hall door suddenly flung open. In the doorway, surrounded by howling wind
and a fierce snowstorm, was a man disheveled and clearly distressed. He had rags over his feet instead of shoes, a long beard, a coffee pot hanging from a strap on one side,
and a rifle over the other. After standing there for a second,
he began to beg them for help. This man's name was Alfred Packer. General Charles Adams, who oversaw the agency,
got his men to help Alfred to a table with some food, and because he was starving,
ate so quickly that he threw up. Then, over the first of many whiskeys, he told them
about his horrific journey over the mountains. He explained that the others with him
had become too exhausted to continue, that he got snow blindness and frostbite, and he'd
been left behind to fend for himself. For months afterward, he'd eaten rabbits,
roots, and rosebuds, and it was only his experience as a guide
that got him out alive. Several months earlier, when the party that
Alfred eventually joined set out from Bingham Canyon in Utah on November 20th,
1873, they were part of a group of 20. They didn't know each other initially, except for the fact
that they all wanted to be rich. This group was traveling to the newly found goldfields
near Breckenridge in Colorado, which is a place where the newspapers claimed
anyone with any sense could make a fortune. And in fact, when they started out, Alfred
wasn't actually with them. The group happened to bump into him south of
Salt Lake City about 25 miles into their journey. Alfred asked them where they were going, and they
told him they were heading for the goldfields. Alfred then offered his services. He claimed he was a guide and knew the territory
between Utah and Brackenridge well. At first, they weren't sure about him
because he seemed a little odd, but they thought having someone who knew
where they were going was helpful, so they agreed to take him on. Unfortunately, Alfred actually had no idea
where he was going, and to call him only a little bit odd was being nice. However, he wasn't lying completely. He had worked as a guide for a few months;
he just wasn't very good at it. He had a habit of getting lost and tended
to get into arguments with his clients. He also had a reputation for stealing
from people and lying, so those who knew him either didn't like him
or didn't trust him, or both. When he was younger, Alfred served in the Union Army
during the Civil War and enlisted twice, but his service only lasts a few months each time
because he had epilepsy and was prone to seizures. This led to him being honorably discharged both times, and after being discharged, and in addition
to being a guide, for a time, he was employed driving horses
and other draft animals across the West. He also worked as a hunter and a range hand,
and even did odd jobs for mining companies. He even tried mining in Colorado, but unfortunately,
none of these jobs lasted long because he had such a bad attitude. No one could trust him, and he was
constantly getting fired. In any case, after offering to be a guide to the group in 1873, Alfred would manage to get them as far as
just outside Montrose by getting lucky. But this first 260 miles or so hadn't been easy either. A couple of winters earlier, parts of the western
and midwestern US had been hit by the lowest temperatures on record. 1873 wasn't all that much better either, and the journey from Utah to Colorado
was tough and slow. The trail they were following was covered in
heavy snow, slowing down the wagons, making it almost impossible to stick to a path. They followed a compass for a while,
but eventually got lost anyway, and then by January, they were completely out of food. This forced them to begin eating horse feed,  and even thinking about eating the horses themselves. And if that wasn't bad enough,
they had to put up with Alfred. They would later describe him as greedy,
lazy, and constantly fighting with someone. By then, too, it was obvious that he wasn't
the seasoned guide he claimed to be. A few weeks later, on January 21st,
most of them had all but given up when they stumbled across the camp of a
Native American band known as the Utes, led by a man named Chief Ouray
in a valley just outside Montrose. Contrary to popular belief, relations between
Native Americans and prospectors weren't often hostile. So even though the men looked terrible,
or possibly because they looked so terrible, Chief Ouray gave the men food and offered them shelter. He even suggested that they stay with him
until the weather got better. And the group knew that the next part of the journey
would be just as challenging. They still had roughly 120 more miles
and the San Juan Mountains to cross. To make matters worse, the weather
hadn't improved by February. Chief Ouray even told them that no Ute
would try to make that journey in those conditions; it would be certain death. The safest thing to do was to accept the
chief's offer and wait the winter out. Unfortunately, they were also worried that other
groups would get all of the gold before they got there. They were just one of many groups
who were making the trip in search of riches. So, after a meeting, the group decided
to leave half the party behind to look after the horses and wagons till spring. At the same time, the other half will try to make
their way to Los Piños Indian Agency. Chief Ouray realized there was no way
he could talk them out of it, so he gave them some directions to help them
get over the mountains in one piece. He said the best bet was to drop down to the Gunnison River
and follow it before going north to the agency. Alfred, on the other hand, was insistent it would be better to cross the mountains directly,
rather than going around. He claimed he knew that area,
and that way was a lot quicker. And for some reason, five of the men believed him. The chief then gave each of the groups food, and then the group that didn't have
Alfred in it set off along the river. And just as the chief had warned them,
the journey was brutal in the cold. The freezing winter made following the river difficult, and the food they had ran out long
before they reached the agency. They would have even starved to death if they hadn't been found by some cowhands
working in the area. These men then fed them and let them stay
with them at their cattle camp until spring. In April, when the weather improved, these four men
finally made their way to the agency and got there in May. And to their surprise, Alfred had already
been there and left, but only Alfred; none of the others had been with him. According to the expedition's leader,
after leaving the Ute, Alfred's party followed the river on horseback
until the horses couldn't get any further. The leader then offloaded their provisions
and walked the horses back to the Ute camp. It's thought that they continued to walk
down the river a bit further and then took a path high into the mountains. Importantly, when the leader dropped them off, he knew they didn't have enough supplies
to get to the agency, but he'd just had enough of arguing with Alfred. Afterward, they only had about 14 days of food;
nothing they needed for a winter hike in the mountains. Their clothes weren't adequate to keep them warm, and they had no snowshoes or flints,
and hardly any matches. They only had a few rifles, one pistol,
a hatchet, and some knives. After the expedition lead turned back, no one heard
from any of these men again until months later, when Alfred burst into the mess hall at the agency. And from the beginning, something seemed strange. Alfred told the workers he was starving,
but by the look of them, he'd been eating quite a lot of rabbits and rosebuds. They'd seen men trapped in the wilderness before,
and they were usually all but walking skeletons. They typically didn't show up with a bloated face
and a well-fed belly like Alfred had. When Alfred claimed to be feeling a bit better, he headed
to the nearest town, which was Saguache. While he was there, he got himself a room and a saloon, and spent over a hundred dollars on drinking and gambling.
That's around $3,800 in 2023. Then he spent another $78 in the general store,
and when he drank, he often gave conflicting stories about what had happened. Some people even said that he had a different
wallet every time he went out, and he never seemed to run out of cash. He'd sold his rifle when he was back at the agency, but all he got for that was $10;
it didn't explain the rest of the money. He didn't even seem to be any good at gambling. Preston Nutter was the man who arrived
at the agency in May, and he was the leader of the other party
that followed the river. After leaving the agency, he also went to
Saguache in search of answers. And probably because he already knew Alfred was a liar, Preston was immediately suspicious of Alfred's story. He told General Adams that there was no way
the other men would have left him for dead. The rifle he'd sold belonged to an old man
who was with Alfred's group, and the pipe Alfred had left behind was owned
by another one of the men named Shannon Bell. In addition to all of that, when Alfred originally
joined the group, he had no money. Following this revelation, the general
sent a man on horseback to get Alfred and bring him in for questioning. When Alfred got back, the general
and his men wanted to know where Alfred had gotten the money. They also wanted to know why he had
some of the other men's things, and how he'd managed to not only survive
the mountains, but to turn up well-fed. In response, Alfred first claimed that
he'd gotten his feet wet and cold and had to stay by the fire while
the others went to look for food. When they didn't return,
he assumed they'd abandoned him. To Preston though, the story made no sense;
the other men were prospectors. Even if he wasn't a great guide,
he was better than no guide. Eventually, a council was formed to get
to the bottom of everything. Then right as the meeting was starting, two members of the Ute tribe arrived
at the agency with pieces of flesh which they claimed came from a human
found on a hill close to the agency. Upon seeing this, Alfred panicked and then
fainted, and then when he woke up he begged for mercy, and as he sobbed,
told a different story. Before beginning though, he was reported as saying: "It would not be the first time that people had been
obliged to eat each other when they were hungry." Alfred then went on to explain that ten days
into their journey, they'd run out of food. The oldest man had died first, and because
they were all so hungry, the others ate him and took his rifle. Five days later, another man died,
and they ate him as well. They also went through his pockets and found $133. Not long after that, another man who was with them died, but Alfred wasn't there when it happened
because he was getting wood for the fire. The remaining men then ate him too. Soon after that, the owner of the pipe,
Shannon Bell, shot the remaining men. Then, he and Alfred carried some of him with them for food on their journey and then covered up the rest. Two weeks later, Shannon tried to kill him too. Alfred claimed that Shannon went mad
and attacked him, and so in self defense, Alfred shot him. Then a little while later,
he managed to stumble into the agency. General Adams had this full confession written down, and he made Alfred sign it as a sworn statement. Obviously, Preston didn't believe any of this; he was sure that Alfred had killed them
and stolen their things. It got so heated that at one point,
Preston dragged Alfred outside, and if others hadn't intervened, he would have
killed him then and there. After the scuffle was broken up,
Alfred was arrested for manslaughter and imprisoned in a log cabin
owned by the sheriff of Saguache. When summer came, General Adams
took Alfred and some of his men into the mountains to try to find and retrieve the bodies, but they couldn't find anything, so Alfred
was returned to his cell. Later in August, while Alfred was waiting for trial, an illustrator named John Randolph
was travelling over the mountains. As he came down a pass to reach Lake City, he walked by a tributary of the Gunnison River
close to the spot where Alvin had previously claimed he'd left Shannon. There, he noticed something sticking out of the ground. Immediately, he was hit by a terrible smell, but if the stench was hard to take,
what he saw was even worse. He found five men, each in a different state
of decomposition, and it was clear they'd all met violent ends. One of the men was little more than bones, as if
animals had gotten to him afterward. Two of the men had clearly been hit in the
head with something blunt. Another man, who was identified as Shannon Bell, had been stripped to the bones
except for his hands and feet. It was clear he suffered a blunt force injury
to his head as well. From what remained, it was fairly clear that there was
a deliberate removal of the edible portions, and apart from the first man, it didn't look
as though this was done by animals. Upon stumbling on this horrific scene,
John stopped to make a sketch of it, and then he continued on and told
the authorities in Lake City. It won't show the sketch here, but it is still available online. A little while later, a team of 20 volunteers
set off and retrieved the bodies. Upon examination, the coroner was sure they'd all been
killed by a blow to the head while they were asleep. None of them had any defensive wounds or injuries,
and they all had similar markings on their skulls. Other evidence only made things worse for Alfred. All the men had rags under their feet, meaning
they were probably hungry enough to have eaten the leather in their shoes
when they ran out of everything else. There was also a track to a makeshift shelter,
leading them to speculate that maybe Alfred had killed them for their possessions, got stuck there when the weather turned bad,
and then eaten them to survive. Because of these findings, it was expected
that Alfred's charges would be upgraded from manslaughter
to first-degree murder. However, before this could happen,
someone slipped Alfred a key, a penknife, and some food so he could escape. To this day, it's not clear exactly who was responsible, but either way, at some point, Alfred slipped out of his cell
and wasn't seen again for nine years. In 1883, one of the original prospectors
who stayed the winter with Chief Ouray a decade earlier had set up a shop
selling supplies in Cheyenne, Wyoming. On March 11th, a man approached him
 looking to stock up for a planned trip, and introduced himself as John Schwartze. To the man, John seemed familiar, and for a second, he thought it might be the same John Schwartze
he'd spent time with at a Native American camp all those years ago. But when he looked again, he realized
it wasn't John; it was Alfred. After the interaction, the man went on to tell
the local sheriff he spotted a criminal, and Alfred was eventually arrested and taken to Denver. General Adams then traveled up to confirm it was Alfred, and after he had confirmed it, he took him away for trial, and he asked Alfred once again what had
really happened all those years ago. This time, Alfred came up with
what would be his final story, one he more or less stuck to until he died. When Alfred's group left Ouray's camp, they didn't
have anywhere near enough food. The amount was basically only enough
for a single grown man to eat for a week. Then on top of that, after two or three days,
they were hit by a brutal snowstorm. They continued to trek through this until
they got to the base of a mountain. Then beyond that was a deep valley,
but on the other side of the valley, the snow was so deep they could barely walk. This forced them to get to higher ground,
and already by day four, they only had about a pint of flour left. For the next ten days or so, they lived
only on rosebuds and pine gum as they followed a ridge to stay out of the deeper snow. Apparently, several of the men were in rough shape
by then and would cry out every night and pray to God, hoping they could escape
the mountains alive. Eventually, they came over the main ridge
and descended in camp by a river. They followed this stream for a day
until they reached a lake, possibly Lake San Cristobal,
that at the time was frozen over. They decided to cross the lake to where
a few trees could be used for shelter, and by then, they were exhausted,
and tensions were rising. And while some of the men were
desperate and breaking down, Shannon Bell was feeling something different;
he was furious. He was mad at Alfred for getting them lost, and at the others for how pathetic
he thought they were acting. And then one morning, Shannon was
acting stranger than usual. According to Alfred, it seemed like he
either had a plan to survive, or was going insane, or maybe both. That morning, he told Alfred to go out on his own and explore higher up the mountain to see
if there was any way of getting across. So Alfred took a pistol and set off, but all he found
were steep slopes and more snow; both of which weren't very helpful. He would even admit to the general for the first time
that although he was kind of a guide, he didn't really know what he was doing, and he
didn't know that side of the mountains. It took him all day to scout ahead and come back,
and then when he got back, he found Shannon sitting by the fire,
eating a piece of meat. Alfred then stopped and looked around,
and he could see a man lying there a little ways from the fire, and it was clear
what had happened. Then he looked back towards Shannon and saw the
other three men lying around the fire, not moving. Then he slowly approached the fire, and upon noticing
Alfred, Shannon rushed at him with a hatchet, but he managed to shoot Shannon in the stomach
before he could reach him. Alfred then finished him off after he fell to the ground. Later that evening would be the worst night of Alfred's life. In a letter written later, he asked if anyone
could imagine how he felt that night. In his own words, he was surrounded by:  "the midnight horrors of starvation
as well as those of utter isolation." He also claimed he felt like he was losing his sanity, and he started to understand what happened to Shannon
because it was beginning to happen to him. In another letter, he even said: "The greatest wonder is that I ever
returned to a rational condition." The next morning, he tried to follow
his tracks from the day before, but between the snow and the exhaustion,
he was forced to turn back. So next, he made a small shelter out of wood
and branches to keep warm, but that didn't do anything to satisfy
his ever-growing hunger. The group had spent enough time out there
already for him to know that hunting wasn't a reliable source of food. So eventually, in complete desperation,
he picked up the piece of meat Shannon had been eating, cooked it for a while,
and then bit into it. Almost right away, the horror of what he was doing
was overcome by the relief of eating food, and he knew what he had to do to survive. He would then go on to spend another
two months there in the little shelter, surviving off the rest of his party. 60 days later, he spotted an avalanche
that left yellow clay behind. This was an indication that he'd been
in an area known as Slumgullion Pass, which is known for its yellow color,
and was named Slumgullion because it reminded early settlers of Slumgullion stew. So finally, now in early spring, Alfred had an idea
of where to go, and set off up the mountain again. Before he did, he gathered some of the remaining meat
and wrapped it so he could eat it while he walked. He also checked the pockets of the
other men before he left, which is when he found the money
he later spent in Saguache. And like the others, he'd already eaten his shoes,
so he wrapped his feet in cloth and sometimes, he had to stop because
his feet began to freeze. When that happened, he stopped
and lit a fire to warm them. Then when he got close to the agency,
he ate the last pieces of meat and possibly dropped some,
which were later found by the Ute. He also admitted that when he went out with
General Adams search party a decade earlier, he took the men as far as the mountains
opposite the camp and did all he could to stop them from going further. He claimed that he really did want to take
them further to show them the truth, but even more than that, he didn't want to go back
and be reminded of the horror he'd been through. Alfred also told them that the reason
that he'd escaped and ran from trial was because he feared that a mob
might get past his guard and kill him. He'd already nearly been killed by Preston Nutter, and so he thought, sooner or later,
someone would finish the job. After escaping, he went to Arkansas using
a fake name and worked on a ranch, before eventually moving on to Arizona, and then
finally traveling to Cheyenne where he was found. And that's the story that Alfred consistently told
until the day he died. When his trial finally began, there were several parts
of this story that were called into question. In particular, people were convinced that everything
was deliberate and premeditated. It was thought that he had deliberately led the men astray with the intent to steal their possessions
by any means necessary. His harrowing survival story afterward was just an
attempt to cover up his actions after the crime. The prosecution would end up bringing in witness
after witness to support this idea. Some of them were part of the original group
of people who set out from Utah. One of them was Preston, who testified that Alfred was always trying to find out
how much money they had. Other witnesses were brought in to
testify to Alfred's behavior after he got to Saguache, and the different
accounts he told of the events. Then when Alfred finally took the stand,
his testimony didn't help his case either. He rambled on for six hours and admitted
to eating the other members of the party, but swore that he only killed Shannon;
Shannon was responsible for everything else. After all the evidence was presented,
the jury would go on to find Alfred guilty of premeditated murder, theft, and several other charges. He was then sentenced to be hanged for his crimes. Before that could happen though,
Alfred's lawyers discovered a technicality. Colorado became a state in 1876,
and prior to its statehood, Colorado Territory didn't have a statute
under which he could be tried for murder. It wasn't until after the crime had
taken place that Colorado State established the specific laws for which
he was being tried for. Because of this, the conviction was overturned, and he had to be retried for manslaughter
instead of murder. In this new trial, Alfred again pled not guilty
and stuck to his story, but this case was even more damning for him. The prosecution brought in hunters who said there was
plenty of food where they were, even in a bad winter. Game, rabbits, deer, and plenty more
would have been easy to hunt, even by someone as inexperienced as Alfred. They even went as far as to claim that the
cannibalism had to have been by choice because food would have been so plentiful in the area. In addition to that, it was argued that at the very least, even if he wasn't some malicious monster
who premeditated the whole thing, he did still lead the group astray
by hiking that more dangerous route in the winter under the guise of being a guide. In the best case scenario, he was extremely negligent, and so he was eventually found guilty
of voluntary manslaughter. For this conviction, he received 40 years in prison,
which was the maximum of 8 years per man. At the time, this was the longest prison sentence
handed down in US history. After being imprisoned, Alfred wrote to anyone he could, claiming the sentence was unjust,
that he'd only killed Shannon, and that the jury was full of biased and prejudiced people. Eventually, Alfred's story got to a woman named Polly Pry. Polly Pry was a reporter for the Denver Post, and unlike most people, after hearing Alfred's story,
she kind of believed him. Because of this, she began to use her position
as a reporter to try to help him. She would end up writing stories about him,
making him out to be a man of the people. She claimed he was just an ex-soldier who
had been persecuted by the establishment, and was someone who was just in the wrong place
at the wrong time, and survived the sort of horrors that
most of us couldn't imagine. She claimed his sentence was only so harsh
because of the cannibalism, but anyone would have done the same in that situation. And incredibly, over time, her stories made such an impact that local businesses started to arrange
petitions for his release. Then, finally, after enough pressure,
the Colorado governor paroled Alfred in 1901, just 18 years into his sentence. In the over a century since the story took place, several different groups have done separate
forensic analysis of the remains and compared them to Alfred's account
of what happened. The conclusions of these groups have tended
to lean in favor of Alfred being guilty, with some showing defensive wounds
on some of the bones of the group, contrary to what should have been there
if Alfred was telling the truth. Like for example, one group found marks
across the forearms of Shannon Bell, which indicate he may have defended
himself from an attack. In Alfred's account, Shannon was only shot once,
and then finished quickly. At the same time, there also seems to be some
evidence that corroborates Alfred's story. In 1994, an 1862 Colt revolver
was found at the site of the murders. It was still loaded with three .38-caliber bullets, and these bullets matched some fragments
of lead found in Shandon Bell's hip, suggesting that at least part of Alfred's story
may have been true. After prison, Alfred at least seemed to be a changed man. He went on to work at the Denver Post
as a guard for a while, and people described him as kind,
modest, and even charitable; far from the grumpy, greedy, and untrustworthy
guy he'd been in the past. He eventually moved out to a city known as Littleton, where he bought a copper mine,
and went back into prospecting. He eventually died in 1907 at 65 years old,
and rumor has it he was a vegetarian when he died. I would take that with a grain of salt, however. So what do you think happened? Do you think
Alfred was telling the truth? In some ways, it seems so clear he was lying,
but in others, maybe not. Although he had a bad reputation, it's quite a big jump to go from petty theft
to what he was eventually accused of. Was he really capable of what is thought to have
happened in those mountains in the middle of winter, or was he just a victim of circumstance? Let me know down in the comments
what you think happened. If you made it this far, thank you so much for watching. If you have a story suggestion, feel free to submit it
to the form found in the description, and hopefully, I will see you in the next one.

Chief Ouray warned them that no Ute would try that crossing in those conditions and that it would mean certain death.

Packer went to Saguache, where he spent over $100 on drinking and gambling and another $78 at a general store.
The source says his drinking and gambling spree would be about $3,800 in 2023 money.

Preston went to Saguache to investigate and immediately suspected Packer’s story was false.
Preston told General Adams that the other men would not have left Packer for dead.
Preston said the rifle Packer sold belonged to an old man in the party and that Packer’s pipe belonged to Shannon Bell.
Preston also pointed out that Packer had no money when he originally joined the party.
General Adams sent a mounted man to bring Packer in for questioning.
When asked where he got his money and how he had survived, Packer first said his feet got wet and cold and that he stayed by the fire while the others went for food.
Packer said he assumed the others had abandoned him when they did not return.
A council was formed to investigate the matter, and two Ute men then arrived with pieces of flesh they said came from a human body found on a hill near the agency.
Packer panicked, fainted, woke up, begged for mercy, and then gave a different account while sobbing.
Packer reportedly said that it would not be the first time hungry people had been obliged to eat each other.
Packer’s confession said that ten days into the journey the group ran out of food.
Packer said the oldest man died first, and the others ate him and took his rifle.
Packer said another man died five days later, and the others ate him and found $133 in his pockets.
Packer said Shannon Bell then shot the remaining men.
Packer said he and Shannon carried some of the dead man’s flesh for food and covered up the rest.
Packer said Shannon later tried to kill him too, and that he shot Shannon in self-defense after Shannon attacked him with madness.
General Adams had this confession written down and made Packer sign it as a sworn statement.
Preston dragged Packer outside during the argument, and others had to intervene to stop Preston from killing him.
Packer was arrested for manslaughter and imprisoned in a log cabin owned by the sheriff of Saguache.
In summer, General Adams took Packer and some men into the mountains to search for the bodies, but they found nothing.
While Packer was waiting for trial in August, illustrator John Randolph traveled over the mountains near Lake City.
Randolph saw something sticking out of the ground near a tributary of the Gunnison River close to where Packer had said he left Shannon.
Randolph found five dead men in different states of decomposition.
One of the bodies was nearly reduced to bones, apparently after animals had gotten to it.
Two of the men had blunt-force injuries to the head.
Another body was identified as Shannon Bell, who had been stripped to the bones except for his hands and feet and also had a blunt head injury.
The remains suggested deliberate removal of the edible parts, and except for the first body, the damage did not look like animal scavenging.
Randolph sketched the scene and reported it to authorities in Lake City.
A volunteer team of 20 men later recovered the bodies.
The coroner concluded that the men had been killed by blows to the head while asleep.
None of the bodies had defensive wounds, and their skulls had similar markings.
The men had rags under their feet, suggesting they may have eaten the leather from their shoes after running out of other food.
A track to a makeshift shelter led investigators to suspect that Packer killed the men for their possessions, became stranded, and then ate them to survive.
Packer’s charges were expected to be upgraded from manslaughter to first-degree murder.
Someone gave Packer a key, a penknife, and some food, and he escaped from custody before the charges could be upgraded.
Packer escaped from his cell and was not seen again for nine years.
In 1883, one of the original prospectors who had stayed with Chief Ouray opened a supply shop in Cheyenne, Wyoming.
On March 11, a man calling himself John Schwartze came to the shop to buy supplies for a planned trip.
The shop owner realized the customer was actually Alfred Packer.
The man reported seeing Packer to the local sheriff, and Packer was arrested and taken to Denver.
General Adams later confirmed that the arrested man was Packer and took him away for trial.
When Adams again asked what had happened, Packer gave a final story that he kept more or less until he died.
In Packer’s final story, the group left Chief Ouray’s camp with barely enough food for one grown man for one week.
Packer said that after two or three days they were hit by a brutal snowstorm.
He said they kept trekking until they reached the base of a mountain and then a deep valley with snow so deep they could barely walk.
Packer said they climbed to higher ground and by day four had only about a pint of flour left.
Packer said that for about the next ten days they lived only on rosebuds and pine gum while following a ridge to stay above the deep snow.
Packer said several of the men cried out at night and prayed to escape the mountains alive.
Packer said the party eventually crossed the main ridge and descended into a camp by a river.
Packer said they followed the stream for a day until they reached a frozen lake, possibly Lake San Cristobal.
Packer said they crossed the lake to reach some trees for shelter, and tensions among the men were rising.
Packer said Shannon Bell became furious at him for getting them lost and at the others for acting pathetically.
Packer said Shannon later told him to scout higher up the mountain for a way across.
Packer said he took a pistol and went out alone but found only steep slopes and more snow.
Packer said that on this scouting trip he admitted for the first time to General Adams that he did not really know what he was doing and did not know that side of the mountains.
Packer said it took him all day to scout and return, and when he came back Shannon was sitting by the fire eating a piece of meat.
Packer said he saw a man lying near the fire and saw the other three men lying around it without moving.
Packer said Shannon rushed at him with a hatchet, and Packer shot Shannon in the stomach before finishing him after he fell.
Packer said the night after Shannon’s death was the worst night of his life.
Packer later wrote that he was surrounded by the midnight horrors of starvation and utter isolation.
Packer said he felt himself losing his sanity and beginning to understand Shannon’s condition because it was starting to happen to him too.
Packer later wrote that the greatest wonder was that he ever returned to a rational condition.
Packer said the next morning he tried to follow his tracks from the previous day but had to turn back because of snow and exhaustion.
Packer said he built a small shelter from wood and branches, but it did not satisfy his hunger.
Packer said the relief of eating overcame the horror of cannibalism, and he realized what he had to do to survive.
Packer said he spent another two months in the shelter surviving off the rest of his party.
Sixty days later, Packer said he saw an avalanche that left yellow clay behind, which showed he was in Slumgullion Pass.
Packer said he recognized the area because Slumgullion Pass is known for its yellow color and was named after Slumgullion stew.
Packer said that in early spring he finally knew where to go and set out up the mountain again.
Packer said he wrapped some of the remaining meat for the journey and checked the other men’s pockets, where he found the money he later spent in Saguache.
Packer said he had eaten his shoes, so he wrapped his feet in cloth and had to stop when his feet began to freeze.
Packer said he would light a fire to warm his feet whenever that happened.
Packer said that near the agency he ate the last pieces of meat and may have dropped some that the Ute later found.
Packer said he wanted to take them farther to show them the truth, but he also did not want to go back and be reminded of the horror.
Packer said he escaped because he feared a mob would get past his guard and kill him.
Packer said he had already nearly been killed by Preston Nutter and believed someone would eventually finish the job.
After escaping, Packer said he went to Arkansas under a false name, worked on a ranch, then moved to Arizona and eventually to Cheyenne, where he was found.
Packer’s trial challenged many parts of his story and treated the killings as deliberate and premeditated.
The prosecution argued that Packer intentionally led the men astray to steal their possessions by any means necessary.
The prosecution presented witness after witness to support that theory.
Some prosecution witnesses had been members of the original party that left Utah.
Preston Nutter testified that Packer was always trying to find out how much money the men had.
Other witnesses testified about Packer’s behavior in Saguache and the conflicting stories he told about the events.
When Packer testified, he spoke for six hours and admitted eating the other party members but claimed he only killed Shannon and that Shannon was responsible for everything else.
After the evidence was presented, the jury found Packer guilty of premeditated murder, theft, and several other charges.
Packer was sentenced to hang for his crimes.
Packer’s lawyers discovered that Colorado Territory had no murder statute before Colorado became a state in 1876.
The laws under which Packer was tried for murder were created only after the crime had already happened.
Because of that legal problem, the conviction was overturned and Packer had to be retried for manslaughter instead of murder.
In the new trial, Packer again pleaded not guilty and repeated his story.
The prosecution then brought hunters who said there was plenty of food in the area even in a bad winter.
The hunters said game such as rabbits and deer would have been easy to hunt even for someone as inexperienced as Packer.
Alfred was sentenced to be hanged for his crimes.
Alfred's lawyers discovered a technicality before the hanging could happen.
Before statehood, Colorado Territory did not have a statute under which Alfred could be tried for murder.
Colorado State established the specific laws for the crime after the crime had already taken place.
Because of the lack of a murder statute at the time of the crime, Alfred's conviction was overturned.
The prosecution argued that the cannibalism had to have been by choice because food would have been plentiful in the area.
It was argued that Alfred at least led the group astray by hiking the more dangerous route in winter under the guise of being a guide.
The argument also said that, in the best case scenario, Alfred was extremely negligent.
Alfred was eventually found guilty of voluntary manslaughter.
For the voluntary manslaughter conviction, Alfred received 40 years in prison.
The 40-year sentence was described as the maximum of 8 years per man.
At the time, the 40-year sentence was the longest prison sentence handed down in US history.
After being imprisoned, Alfred wrote to anyone he could and claimed the sentence was unjust.
Alfred claimed that he had only killed Shannon and that the jury was full of biased and prejudiced people.
Alfred's story eventually reached a woman named Polly Pry.
Polly Pry was a reporter for the Denver Post.
After hearing Alfred's story, Polly Pry partly believed him.
She wrote stories about Alfred and portrayed him as a man of the people.
She claimed he was an ex-soldier who had been persecuted by the establishment.
She claimed he was in the wrong place at the wrong time and survived horrors most people could not imagine.
She claimed his sentence was harsh because of the cannibalism, but that anyone would have done the same in that situation.
Over time, Polly Pry's stories persuaded local businesses to arrange petitions for Alfred's release.
After enough pressure, the Colorado governor paroled Alfred in 1901.
Alfred was paroled 18 years into his sentence.
Over the century after the story, several different groups conducted separate forensic analyses of the remains and compared them with Alfred's account.
Those groups tended to conclude that Alfred was guilty.
Some analyses showed defensive wounds on some of the bones of the group.
One group found marks across the forearms of Shannon Bell that indicated he may have defended himself from an attack.
In Alfred's account, Shannon was only shot once and then finished quickly.
In 1994, an 1862 Colt revolver was found at the site of the murders.
The revolver was still loaded with three .38-caliber bullets.
The bullets matched some fragments of lead found in Shannon Bell's hip.
The revolver and bullet match suggested that at least part of Alfred's story may have been true.
After prison, Alfred worked at the Denver Post as a guard for a while.
People described Alfred after prison as kind, modest, and even charitable.
Those descriptions contrasted with his earlier reputation as grumpy, greedy, and untrustworthy.
Alfred later moved to a city known as Littleton.
In Littleton, Alfred bought a copper mine.
Alfred died in 1907 at 65 years old.
There is a rumor that Alfred was a vegetarian when he died.
The narrator says that rumor should be taken with a grain of salt.

📄 Full Source Text (click to expand) ``` In 1874, six men set off into Colorado's San Juan Mountains in the middle of winter with the hopes of reaching some newly discovered goldfields on the other side. Two months later, only a single man emerged from the mountains, but instead of being emaciated as early explorers were often later found, the man looked to be weirdly fed. This is the story of Alfred Packer, also known as the Colorado Cannibal. As a quick note, although the descriptions of the events in this video are fleeting and non-descriptive, they are still disturbing, so viewer discretion is strongly advised. [intro music] On the morning of April 16th, 1874, the men who worked at Los Piños Indian Agency near Saguache, Colorado were sitting and eating breakfast when the mess hall door suddenly flung open. In the doorway, surrounded by howling wind and a fierce snowstorm, was a man disheveled and clearly distressed. He had rags over his feet instead of shoes, a long beard, a coffee pot hanging from a strap on one side, and a rifle over the other. After standing there for a second, he began to beg them for help. This man's name was Alfred Packer. General Charles Adams, who oversaw the agency, got his men to help Alfred to a table with some food, and because he was starving, ate so quickly that he threw up. Then, over the first of many whiskeys, he told them about his horrific journey over the mountains. He explained that the others with him had become too exhausted to continue, that he got snow blindness and frostbite, and he'd been left behind to fend for himself. For months afterward, he'd eaten rabbits, roots, and rosebuds, and it was only his experience as a guide that got him out alive. Several months earlier, when the party that Alfred eventually joined set out from Bingham Canyon in Utah on November 20th, 1873, they were part of a group of 20. They didn't know each other initially, except for the fact that they all wanted to be rich. This group was traveling to the newly found goldfields near Breckenridge in Colorado, which is a place where the newspapers claimed anyone with any sense could make a fortune. And in fact, when they started out, Alfred wasn't actually with them. The group happened to bump into him south of Salt Lake City about 25 miles into their journey. Alfred asked them where they were going, and they told him they were heading for the goldfields. Alfred then offered his services. He claimed he was a guide and knew the territory between Utah and Brackenridge well. At first, they weren't sure about him because he seemed a little odd, but they thought having someone who knew where they were going was helpful, so they agreed to take him on. Unfortunately, Alfred actually had no idea where he was going, and to call him only a little bit odd was being nice. However, he wasn't lying completely. He had worked as a guide for a few months; he just wasn't very good at it. He had a habit of getting lost and tended to get into arguments with his clients. He also had a reputation for stealing from people and lying, so those who knew him either didn't like him or didn't trust him, or both. When he was younger, Alfred served in the Union Army during the Civil War and enlisted twice, but his service only lasts a few months each time because he had epilepsy and was prone to seizures. This led to him being honorably discharged both times, and after being discharged, and in addition to being a guide, for a time, he was employed driving horses and other draft animals across the West. He also worked as a hunter and a range hand, and even did odd jobs for mining companies. He even tried mining in Colorado, but unfortunately, none of these jobs lasted long because he had such a bad attitude. No one could trust him, and he was constantly getting fired. In any case, after offering to be a guide to the group in 1873, Alfred would manage to get them as far as just outside Montrose by getting lucky. But this first 260 miles or so hadn't been easy either. A couple of winters earlier, parts of the western and midwestern US had been hit by the lowest temperatures on record. 1873 wasn't all that much better either, and the journey from Utah to Colorado was tough and slow. The trail they were following was covered in heavy snow, slowing down the wagons, making it almost impossible to stick to a path. They followed a compass for a while, but eventually got lost anyway, and then by January, they were completely out of food. This forced them to begin eating horse feed, and even thinking about eating the horses themselves. And if that wasn't bad enough, they had to put up with Alfred. They would later describe him as greedy, lazy, and constantly fighting with someone. By then, too, it was obvious that he wasn't the seasoned guide he claimed to be. A few weeks later, on January 21st, most of them had all but given up when they stumbled across the camp of a Native American band known as the Utes, led by a man named Chief Ouray in a valley just outside Montros... ```
